correctness.rationale: For any base-3 digit product \(p_3(n)=2^{t(n)}\), odd prodigious n requires \(t(n)=0\), so \(n\pmod9\) belongs to \(\{0,1,3,4\}\), which has no three-member difference-two run. For even n, CRT of \(n\equiv2\pmod4\) and the seven three-digit ternary suffix patterns with >=2 digit-2s gives \(F=\{26,50,62,74,78,98,106\}\pmod{108}\). The forbidden positions in a 54-position even residue cycle are \(\{13,25,31,37,39,49,53\}\); successive circular gaps 12,6,6,2,10,4,14 force every 14-term even progression to hit F. The 13 terms \(108+2j\ (0\le j<13)\) have products [1,2,1,2,4,1,1,2,2,2,4,2,4] dividing each term. Adding \(4\cdot3^K\ (K\ge5)\) prepends ternary digits 11 without changing products, and preserves divisibility by products dividing 4; infinitely many witnesses. check_prodigious.py reproduces exact complete residue cycles and finite witnesses; finite search is not used as an infinite proof.

Its section 3 concerns maximal consecutive runs and thus cannot imply a d=2 extremum. Sanna estimates cardinalities over all integers and supplies no maximal difference-two classification.

originality.rationale: Full primary comparison with Gohn et al. 2022 identifies an uncovered first non-divisor step in the smallest nonbinary base: their Theorem 3 requires \(d\mid b\) with \(d<b/2\), and their Theorem 5 requires even b with \(d=b/2\); \((b,d)=(3,2)\) satisfies neither. Their d=1 maximum of 5 does not imply this \(d=2\) maximum 13. Sanna 2018 treats growth of counting functions, not progression extrema, and OEIS A055471 indexes decimal rather than this ternary invariant. Targeted statement and exact witness searches produced no equivalent. Independent novelty is unproved, and unindexed equivalent work remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed or recent equivalent theorem could exist beyond targeted literature searches.

value.rationale: Exact sharp first missing step (\(d=2\) not dividing \(b=3\)) for a natural family explicitly studied in JIS 2022: the established \((b,d)=(3,1)\) maximum is 5, whereas the new precise \((b,d)=(3,2)\) maximum is 13. The result gives a universal congruence obstruction and infinitely many extremizers, forming a substantive boundary case for study of fixed-step digit-product divisibility, not a routine application of the \(d\mid b\) classification.
